---
title: "Login"
subtitle: "How a web-service token is obtained, verified and stored"
---

Moodle does not hand out API tokens to arbitrary clients. The only route a
normal account has is the one the official mobile app uses:
`admin/tool/mobile/launch.php` issues a token after an interactive login, and
redirects to a custom URL scheme (`moodlemobile://token=...`) that the app is
registered to handle. `src/auth/flow.py` reimplements that handshake and
catches the redirect in a scripted browser instead of an app.

**The password is never seen by this code.** It is typed into a real browser
window on the institution's own SSO page. The code opens the page and watches
for the redirect.

## The handshake

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant C as MoodleAuthenticator
  participant M as Moodle site
  participant B as Browser (Playwright)
  participant U as User
  participant K as OS keyring

  C->>M: POST lib/ajax/service-nologin.php<br/>tool_mobile_get_public_config
  M-->>C: wwwroot, launchurl, typeoflogin, forcedurlscheme
  Note over C: passport = secrets.token_hex(16)
  C->>B: open launch.php?service=…&passport=…&urlscheme=…
  B->>M: GET launch.php
  M-->>B: redirect to SSO
  U->>B: credentials + 2FA on the SSO page
  B->>M: authenticated callback
  M-->>B: 302 → moodlemobile://token=<base64>
  B-->>C: captured URL
  Note over C: base64 → site_hash:::token:::private_token<br/>assert md5(wwwroot + passport) == site_hash
  C->>K: store token, keyed by site URL
```

### Step 0 --- public config

`fetch_public_config()` POSTs `tool_mobile_get_public_config` to
`lib/ajax/service-nologin.php`. No authentication required. It answers four
things that matter:

| Field | Used for |
|---|---|
| `wwwroot` / `httpswwwroot` | The exact root string hashed into the signature |
| `launchurl` | Where to start the handshake |
| `typeoflogin` | `1` = in-app form (unsupported), `2`/`3` = browser login |
| `forcedurlscheme` | A site may override `moodlemobile://` |

A failure here almost always means mobile web services are disabled site-wide,
and the error says so rather than reporting a network problem.

### Step 1 --- the passport

```python
passport = secrets.token_hex(16)
launch_url = f"{launchurl}?service=moodle_mobile_app&passport={passport}&urlscheme={scheme}"
```

The passport is the whole security property of the flow. Moodle returns the
token alongside `md5(wwwroot + passport)`, and only a response to *our* launch
request can carry a hash over *our* passport. That makes a token for a
different site, a replayed old redirect, and a tampered one all detectable.
`begin_login()` mints a fresh passport per attempt, invalidating any previous
one.

### Step 2 --- catching the redirect

Browsers refuse to navigate to an unregistered URL scheme, and *how* they
refuse differs. `BrowserTokenCapture` therefore watches three places at once
and takes whichever fires first:

1. the `Location` header of any 3xx response,
2. `request` and `framenavigated` events for any non-http scheme carrying
   `token=`,
3. the `a#launchapp` fallback link Moodle renders when the redirect cannot
   fire, polled every 500 ms.

The browser is the user's default when Playwright can drive it, meaning
Chrome, Edge, Brave, Vivaldi or Chromium (`src/auth/browser.py` reads the
macOS LaunchServices plist or the Windows `UserChoice` key). A default it
cannot drive, such as Safari or Firefox, falls back to installed Chrome, then
Edge, and from source to Playwright's bundled Chromium.

The browser context is created fresh with no `storage_state` and no user data
directory, and is closed before the function returns --- the SSO session must
not outlive the capture. Playwright's sync API cannot run inside a live asyncio
loop, so the capture is dispatched to a worker thread, which is what makes it
callable from a Jupyter notebook.

If all three strategies miss (some browsers swallow the redirect behind a
native "open app?" dialog), `complete_manual(url)` verifies a URL pasted in by
hand. Same verification path, no browser.

### Step 3 --- verification

```
base64(payload) → "<site_hash>:::<token>[:::<private_token>]"
```

The payload is base64-decoded leniently --- URL-safe alphabet, missing padding
and double percent-encoding all occur in practice --- but with
`validate=True`, because without it `base64` silently skips characters outside
the alphabet and happily decodes garbage.

Then `verify_and_decode` recomputes `md5(candidate + passport)` for each
plausible spelling of the root (with and without trailing slash, since Moodle
hashes whatever its own config holds) and compares with
`secrets.compare_digest`. No match is a hard failure: the token is discarded,
never stored.

### Step 4 --- storage

`TokenStore` writes to the OS credential store via `keyring`, keyed by site URL
so several sites coexist:

| Entry | Service name |
|---|---|
| Web-service token | `zhaw-moodle-token` |
| Private token (file downloads) | `zhaw-moodle-private-token` |
| Anthropic API key | `anthropic-api-key` |

If no working backend exists, `MoodleSession` falls back to `MemoryTokenStore`
and says so --- the token then dies with the process. Nothing is ever written to
a file. Tokens are masked as `abcd...wxyz (40 chars)` by `TokenMask` wherever
they are printed, including in `__repr__`, so a notebook cell cannot echo one.

## Connecting

`MoodleSession.connect()` is the entry point for everything downstream:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  A["connect()"] --> B{"token in keyring?"}
  B -->|yes| C["core_webservice_get_site_info"]
  C -->|valid| D["ready"]
  C -->|"invalidtoken"| E["discard, fall through"]
  B -->|no| E
  E --> F["login(): full SSO handshake"]
  F --> G["verify signature"]
  G --> H["save to keyring"] --> D
```

A stored token is *validated*, not trusted: `get_site_info` is the cheapest
call that proves a token still works, and it doubles as the identity lookup
(`userid`, `fullname`, `sitename`, `downloadfiles`). A revoked token returns
`invalidtoken`, which is treated as "no token" and triggers a fresh login
rather than an error.

## Read-only by construction

Three independent layers, so no single mistake can produce a write:

1. **The service.** `moodle_mobile_app` is what the token is scoped to.
2. **The allowlist.** `MoodleClient` checks every `wsfunction` against
   `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_FUNCTIONS` (25 entries, every one a `*_get_*` read) and
   raises `ValueError` *before* a request is made. A write call cannot be expressed;
   pass `allowed_functions=None` to disable the check deliberately.
3. **HTTPS.** `normalise_site_url` rejects a non-HTTPS site URL and
   `MoodleClient.__init__` refuses to send a token over one.

Moodle reports application errors with HTTP 200 and an `exception`/`errorcode`
body, so `raise_for_status()` sees nothing wrong. `_raise_for_moodle_error`
turns those into `MoodleApiError` and attaches advice for the codes worth
explaining (`ERROR_HINTS` in `config.py`). A non-JSON response is reported by
status code only --- the body is never echoed, since an error page can contain
the token.

## Revoking

```python
session.logout()   # deletes both keyring entries, returns what existed
```

This clears the local credentials only. To invalidate the token server-side,
use *Security keys* in your Moodle profile.
